pamphlet_excerpts: Causes of Dehydration: Dehydration, caused by lack of water in the body, can occur in cold or warm weather, anytime a person is sweating profusely and/or not drinking enough (p. 28).
Preventing Fluid Loss: Avoid dehydration by drinking plenty of fluids and eating enough throughout the day to keep your body well-balanced (p. 28).
Treating Heat Exhaustion: If you become weary or develop a headache or body aches, or if you become confused, rest in the shade and sip water until the symptoms subside (p. 28).
Signs of Frostbite: If the freezing continues, the area will stiffen and become grayish-white in color (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Rest and Sip Water: If you become weary or develop a headache or body aches, or if you become confused, rest in the shade and sip water until the symptoms subside (p. 28).
Step 2 - Identify Frozen Tissue: If the freezing continues, the area will stiffen and become grayish-white in color (p. 28).
Step 3 - Thaw Without Refreezing Risk: To treat the victim, thaw the affected area only if there is no risk of refreezing (p. 28).
Step 4 - Warm With Body Heat: Put cold fingers under the armpit and the warm palm of your hand on frostbitten nose, ears, or cheeks (p. 28).

Tying a Webbing Runner: A piece of webbing can be tied into a loop known as a runner with a water knot (p. 49).
Pre-Sewn Runners and Slings: Webbing can be purchased as a runner or sling and is pre-sewn by the Be layers use tubular webbing to manufacturer (p. 49).

Step 3 - Anchor Securely With Runners: Climbers use runners, or anchor themselves securely (p. 49).
Step 4 - Protect Webbing From Wear: Like all climbing rope, all webbing can be harmed by friction, dirt, and long exposure to sunlight or harsh weather (p. 49).

pamphlet_excerpts: Joining Two Rope Ends: For tying together the ends of two ropes, the most reliable knot is the double fisherman's knot (p. 53).
Forming a Cord Runner: It can also be used to secure the ends of a piece of cord to form a runner (p. 53).
Barrel Stopper Knot: Half of a double fisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).
Aligning Opposing Rope Ends: Lay about 2 feet of the ends of two ropes alongside one another, ends opposite (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Tie a Barrel Stopper: Half of a double fisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).
Step 2 - Overlap Two Rope Ends: Lay about 2 feet of the ends of two ropes alongside one another, ends opposite (p. 53).
Step 3 - Wrap Twice and Thread: Loosely loop one rope end twice around the other, then thread the end of that rope through the loops (p. 53).
Step 4 - Dress and Slide Tight: Carefully tighten the two parts of the knot, then slide them (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Benefits of Proper Fit: Using a harness that fits properly helps make climbing and rappelling safer, more comfortable, and fun (p. 57).
Putting On Seat Harnesses: Commercially made climbing harnesses usually require only that you put your legs through leg loops and then secure the waists trap with a buckle (p. 57).
Two-Finger Leg Loop Check: The leg loops of some harnesses can be adjusted; you should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh (p. 57).
Selecting Non-Adjustable Harnesses: If the harnesses available to you are not adjustable, you will need to choose one that fits your body snugly but not tight enough to restrict circulation (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Adjust the Leg Loops: The leg loops of some harnesses can be adjusted; you should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh (p. 57).

Step 2 - Check Waist and Circulation: If the harnesses available to you are not adjustable, you will need to choose one that fits your body snugly but not tight enough to restrict circulation (p. 57).
Step 3 - Wrap Tubular Webbing Harness: A 30-foot length of nylon tubular webbing can be wrapped around your body and tied in special ways to form a reliable tied harness for climbing (p. 57).
Step 4 - Verify Every Harness Tie: Each tied harness must be tied exactly right every time to ensure your safety (p. 57).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Set Your Brake Hand: Arrange the rope so that your stronger hand (usually your right hand if you are right-handed) will be the brake hand, the hand closest to the free end (p. 65).
Step 2 - Exchange Pre-Climb Signals: Exchange verbal signals (see the boxed text later in this chapter) with a climber (p. 65).
Step 3 - Pull Slack Through Device: As the climber ascends, pull through the belay device any slack that forms in the rope, and let the loose rope pile up next to your feet (p. 65).
Step 4 - Slide the Guide Hand: While holding the rope firmly with your brake hand, slide your guide hand out along the rope (p. 65).

options: A. It keeps chalk dust off your shirt and harness
B. It allows the belayer to see your tie-in knot from the ground
C. It prevents the climbing rope from touching the rock surface
D. It presses your climbing shoes firmly onto footholds and lets your strong leg muscles lift your weight
choices: A. It keeps chalk dust off your shirt and harness
B. It allows the belayer to see your tie-in knot from the ground
C. It prevents the climbing rope from touching the rock surface

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. It presses your climbing shoes firmly onto footholds and lets your strong leg muscles lift your weight

pamphlet_excerpts: Dedicated Climbing Helmet Use: Whenever you are climbing, rappelling, or belaying on rock faces, wear a helmet that has been specifically designed for climbing (p. 42).
Deflecting Falling Rock Debris: A helmet will protect your head against stones and debris falling from above, and may prevent injuries if you collide with a rock face during a fall (p. 42).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a climb, which verbal command tells the belayer to pull in loose rope and hold the climber firmly?

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Calling 'Up rope' tells the belayer to pull in any loose slack, and 'Tension' instructs the belayer to pull the rope tight and lock off to support the climber (p. 66).

options: A. The rope feels slightly stiff after being coiled in a dry closet

C. The rope has been used for three top-rope climbs on an indoor wall

choices: A. The rope feels slightly stiff after being coiled in a dry closet
B. The middle marker tape on the sheath has faded from washing in mild soap

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The white inner core fibers are visible through a torn sheath or you feel a soft flat spot
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Exposed inner core fibers, soft or flat spots, hard lumps, or chemical contamination mean the kernmantle rope's integrity is compromised and it must be retired immediately (p. 46).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the number one rule for the brake hand while belaying a climber or rappeller?

C. Switch brake hands after every five feet of rope movement
D. Wrap the brake strand twice around your wrist for extra grip
choices: A. Keep the brake hand above the belay device to feed slack faster

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Never let go of the brake strand with the brake hand while someone is on belay
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Friction in a belay device depends entirely on the brake hand controlling the free end of the rope, so the brake hand must never leave the rope (p. 64).
